extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in moral aphorisms, social conduct, and polished conversation
extracted.subtask_description: Aphoristic guidance on taste, mind, society, conversation, falsehood, and air/manner — practical rules for being agreeable, polite, and effective in social life. Extracts prescriptive criteria and anti-patterns for comportment and speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lofty mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A lofty mind always thinks nobly; it easily creates vivid, agreeable, and natural fancies, places them in their best light, clothes them with all appropriate adornments, studies others' tastes, and clears away from its own thoughts all that is useless and disagreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate elevated, broad, just, and intelligible thoughts; make imaginings natural and agreeable; tailor presentation to others' tastes; strip away what is useless or disagreeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clever, pliant, winning mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A clever, pliant, winning mind knows how to avoid and overcome difficulties; by bending easily to what it wants, it understands the inclination and temper it is dealing with, and by managing their interests it advances and establishes its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be adaptable and tactful: understand others' temper and interests and use that knowledge to achieve aims without blunt confrontation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-regulated mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A well regulated mind sees all things as they should be seen, appraises them at their proper value, turns them to its own advantage, and adheres firmly to its own opinions as it knows all their force and weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the value and weight of your opinions; stick to them when justified, and convert observations into practical advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between working and business-like mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Some are clever only in what does not concern them, others only in their own business; others know how to turn everything to their own advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether your cleverness applies broadly or only to particular concerns; avoid being competent merely in abstract matters while failing in personal affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious mind can be pleasant
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible to have a serious turn of mind, and yet to talk pleasantly and cheerfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance seriousness with agreeable speech; young persons often mix satire and cheerfulness without seriousness — temper satire with seriousness to avoid disagreeableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid always playing pleasant
rubrics_metrics.description: No part is easier to play than that of being always pleasant; the applause we sometimes receive in censuring others is not worth being exposed to the chance of offending them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek applause through censorious pleasantness that risks offending others; be sincere rather than performatively agreeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire — refined and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire always pleases when it is refined but is dangerous when used too much; it should be allowed when unmixed with spite and when the person satirised can join in the satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire sparingly, ensure it's refined and not malicious; avoid satirising those who cannot or will not appreciate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitfalls of satirical turn without affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unfortunate to have a satirical turn without affecting to be pleased or without loving to jest; it requires much adroitness to continue satirical without falling into extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If naturally satirical, cultivate tact and affectation of pleasure when necessary to avoid cruelty or bluntness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raillery and wit distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Raillery is mirth that shows every object in an absurd light; wit combines more or less softness or harshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between playful raillery and sharper wit; modulate harshness according to audience and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined flattering raillery
rubrics_metrics.description: A refined and flattering raillery only hits the faults persons admit, hides praise under appearance of blame, showing the good while feigning to hide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use raillery to flatter subtly by targeting admitted faults and disguising praise, avoiding exposing unknown faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acute mind vs cunning mind
rubrics_metrics.description: An acute mind always pleases: unfettered, perceives delicate, imperceptible matters. A cunning spirit never goes straight, seeks byeways and short cuts, gives rise to distrust and never reaches greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor direct acute perception over devious cunning; avoid manipulative shortcuts that erode trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ardent vs brilliant mind
rubrics_metrics.description: An ardent (fiery) spirit travels further and faster, while a brilliant mind is sparkling, attractive, accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize different strengths — energy vs polish — and cultivate the form that suits you; brilliance requires accuracy and polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleness of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentleness of mind is an easy and accommodating manner which always pleases when not insipid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be accommodating but avoid being bland; maintain character while being pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind full of details
rubrics_metrics.description: A mind full of details devotes itself to managing the smallest particulars; though usually limited to little matters, when combined with greatness these qualities raise a mind above others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value attention to detail, and where possible combine it with broader vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bel esprit perversion and epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'Bel Esprit' is perverted — many bad poets and tedious authors are so called; epithets vary by tone and manner which writing cannot convey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of superficial labels of wit; tone and manner (lost in writing) matter in judging esprit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: There are tones and manners that make phrases of 'wit' express different orders of mind; one can have one kind, several, or every variety of wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop variety in wit; avoid relying on a single comic or rhetorical device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: taste vs liking
rubrics_metrics.description: The word taste has different meanings: attraction for certain objects vs the faculty that makes us distinguish the qualities we judge by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between personal liking and critical taste; don't conflate mere preference with refined judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good taste rare and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Good taste that can accurately set the value of particulars and of all things is very rare; our knowledge is too limited for perfect discernment except in matters not concerning us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limitations of taste; be humble about sweeping judgments and confine confident evaluation to familiar domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste influenced by self-love and fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Our taste is guided by self-love, temper, example, and fashion; few have a taste independent of friends' influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against conforming blindly to fashion or friends; strive for independent discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society: hide preference and humour others
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone seeks pleasure and advantage at others' expense; we should discover means to hide this selection — make our pleasure that of other persons, humour never wound their self-love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In society, disguise self-preference by actively promoting others' pleasure and protecting their self-love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern society by sense, temper, and consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Society would not hold by minds alone; it must be governed by good sense, temper, and consideration between persons living together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate temperance and mutual consideration to sustain social relations beyond mere intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to opposites and avoid instructing
rubrics_metrics.description: When united with persons opposite in temper, those advantaged should not abuse superiority or let it be perceived they serve to instruct others; instead show need to be guided and accommodate to others' feelings and interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid condescension; lead by example and accommodation rather than overt instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of action in society
rubrics_metrics.description: To make society pleasant, each should retain freedom of action — be able to separate oneself without changing the society; people are bored when they feel unable even to bore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect personal autonomy; allow others space and avoid obliging someone to constantly entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaisance with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaisance is essential but should have limits — becomes slavery when extreme; render consent so friends believe they follow your opinion when you follow theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be obliging but not servile; manage deference so others feel empowered while you preserve freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgive and conceal friends' faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Excuse faults born with friends if they are less than their good qualities; avoid showing what they have said or left unsaid; try to make them perceive faults so they correct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privately help friends improve; publicly conceal minor faults and avoid exposing them for amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary politeness among gentlemen
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain kind of politeness prevents rude, unrefined figures of speech used thoughtlessly in heated opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain refined language and self-control to keep discourse civil, especially in disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence in intercourse: equal and discreet
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentlemen's intercourse requires confidence equal on both sides; each should appear sincere and discreet so nothing imprudent is feared being said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be both sincere and discreet; reciprocity of trust is essential for honest exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety in wit to please
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be variety in wit; those with only one kind cannot please for long unless they take different roads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop multiple comedic or rhetorical approaches; avoid repetitiveness which bores company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and avert friends' annoyances
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate what pleases friends, be useful to them to exempt them from annoyance; when you cannot avert evils, seem to participate, obliterate gently, and place agreeable objects instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice empathy and proactive help; replace unpleasantness with mild, agreeable diversions instead of blunt correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen more than speak in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Few are agreeable because each thinks more of what he desires to say than of what others say; we make bad listeners when we want to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize listening, give speakers time, enter into their mind and taste, praise what's praiseworthy; never contradict or interrupt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk about subjects others like
rubrics_metrics.description: To please, talk on subjects that interest others; avoid disputes on indifferent matters, seldom ask questions, and never let them see you pretend to be better informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be audience-centered: choose topics they enjoy, avoid one-upmanship and unnecessary probing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yield to reasonable opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not wrong to retain reasonable opinions, but yield to reason wherever it appears and from whatever side; follow reason without opposing others or seeming to ignore them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open-minded and graceful in changing views when presented with sound arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leading conversation and over-arguing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is dangerous to seek always to lead conversation, and to push a good argument too hard; civility often hides half its understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dominating discussion or humiliating opponents; allow space and preserve civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't talk too long or of one subject
rubrics_metrics.description: We displease when we speak too long and too often of one subject, or try to turn conversation to what we think instructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise, vary topics, stop where others wish, and respect conversational boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone and subject to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak more or less seriously and on more or less abstruse subjects according to the temper and understanding of those you talk with; choose time and manner suitable to condition, sex, talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust formality, complexity, and content to the listener's capacity and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to be silent
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe place, occasion, and temper; there is eloquent silence which approves or condemns, a silence of discretion and of respect — there is a tone, air, and manner which renders everything agreeable or vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use silence strategically; avoid filling every pause and know when quiet speaks louder than words.

rubrics_metrics.name: General maxim for conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: The safest rule: listen much, speak little, and say nothing that will ever give ground for regret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt restraint in speech as a default social policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and ubiquity of falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: We are false in different ways: some wish to appear what they are not, some deceive themselves, some have true understanding but false taste, etc.; falseness is universal in corners of mind or taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of varied self-deceptions and falsities; examine motives for bias or inauthenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of falseness: uncertain qualities and self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: Falseness arises because our qualities and tastes are uncertain and confused; self-love flatters us and follows what others follow without considering suitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counteract self-love and unreflective conformity by critical self-examination and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish good in abstract vs good for oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentleness should approve what deserves to be approved, but distinguish between what is good in the abstract and what is good for ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reason to judge suitability of things for oneself rather than blindly admiring universal merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let reason and good sense fix value
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow reason and good sense to determine taste and the importance to give things; nearly all are deceived in price and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rational evaluation, not vanity or envy, to assess worth; avoid praising what does not suit you merely because it is admired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air and manner: be natural
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an air which belongs to each individual's figure and talents; we lose it when we abandon it to assume another. We should try to find what air is natural and never abandon it, but make it perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate your natural manner instead of imitating others; refine what is innate rather than adopting alien airs that breed falsity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitating others introduces falsity and uncertainty, and what suits one person will not suit another; there are no universal good copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wholesale imitation; adapt only useful habits that harmonize with your nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend acquired qualities with nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquired qualities should agree with our natural qualities; they extend and increase what nature gave, but should be united and blended so they cannot be separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When learning manners or styles, integrate them organically with your natural disposition to avoid affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use different styles for different contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not speak of all subjects in one tone; we do not march at the head of a regiment as we walk on a promenade; use the style suitable to the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modulate voice, demeanor, and diction to suit context and activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming airs above appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Many assume airs of rank or dignity prematurely; dignity that is too marked and not united with natural manner is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display dignity proportionate to genuine status and integrate it with natural manners to avoid ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform air and manner to appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: People often cannot conform air and manners with their appearance, nor style and words with thoughts; those who try to appear what they are not displease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure coherence between appearance, manner, language, and inner character to achieve pleasing presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many pleasing with less ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Thousands with good qualities are displeasing because they wish to appear what they are not; thousands pleasing with far less abilities because they are what they appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity and congruence often matter more than raw ability for social charm.
